Science.title: Webb reveals dynamic panorama of star formation, including smallest known brown dwarfs
Science.summary: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images released to date from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range and revealing new insights about the star-formation process.

Science.title: Supermassive black hole winds are 100 times more powerful than scientists thought
Science.summary: Astronomers have discovered that winds from a supermassive black hole are about 100 times more powerful than previously thought. XRISM observations showed the resulting turbulence spreading roughly 300,000 light-years, extending far beyond the black hole’s host galaxy. The energy involved rivals several billion supernova explosions, revealing just how dramatically black holes can influence the space around them.

Science.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.

Science.title: UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile

However, how chromatin is organized and condensed to form mitotic chromosomes has long remained a major question in genetics and cell biology.

Science.title: Great Salt Lake's ancient past reveals how quickly fresh water can disappear

Mountain ranges would become islands, and the new shoreline would move far beyond its current boundary.

This often requires higher antibiotic doses, increasing the risk of adverse effects and antibiotic resistance.

Science.title: History is being rewritten at an archaeological site in Morocco. What the discovery of an ancient wall tells us

Science.title: Disordered atoms steer shared light pulses by matching motion and timing
Science.summary: A research team at the Institute of Applied Physics at TU Darmstadt has shown for the first time that atoms that are completely disordered and in constant motion can nevertheless emit jointly directed light preferentially in one direction—even though neither the atoms nor their environment exhibit a direction—and that the strength of this asymmetry can be specifically adjusted. The paper is published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Science.title: Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
Science.summary: Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating.

Science.title: Greyhound racing just turned 100, and says its dogs are fine. But are they?
Science.summary: This year, greyhound racing in Britain turns 100 years old. The first race took place on July 24, 1926, in Manchester, where six dogs chased a mechanical hare around a track.

Science.title: South American 'Pompeii': Volcanic eruption 22 million years ago preserved a snapshot of the Andes forming
Science.summary: An enormous volcanic eruption buried a snapshot of the baby Andes mountains, revealing a slow-and-steady growth rate.

Science.title: Drought-flood alternation under climate change
Science.summary: Climate change is increasing the frequency of both droughts and floods, meaning back-to-back extreme events are also on the rise. These rapidly alternating crises can harm people in complex ways. For example, back-to-back climate extremes can stress crops, reducing yields.

Science.title: We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment
Science.summary: AI is unlikely to launch a Hollywood-style war against us. Rather, the biggest danger of AI is that it will disappoint us, says Andrew Rogoyski .

Science.title: This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
Science.summary: Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.

Science.title: Not all roads lead to Rome: Research challenges what we think we know about Roman roads
Science.summary: A multidisciplinary team of researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark, Queen Mary University of London and other European institutions analyzed a data set representing almost 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles) of Roman roads across the former empire, creating the most detailed quantitative picture yet of how the Roman road network was structured.

Science.title: New peanut genome map uncovers hidden gene, boosts dense-planting yields 20%
Science.summary: An international team that includes researchers from Murdoch University's Centre for Crop and Food Innovation (CCFI) has built the most comprehensive genetic map of the peanut yet and used this new genomic resource to breed a higher-yielding dwarf peanut line.

Science.title: 3D food printing of balanced vegetarian dishes from rice and lentil flours
Science.summary: Rice and lentils are a pairing that goes a long way back, whether as khichdi in India or mujaddara in the Middle East. On its own, each is a source of incomplete protein, short on certain essential amino acids—but paired together, they fill each other's gaps, and lentils also blunt white rice's high glycemic index.

Science.title: 'The violence leaves a mark': How satellites are helping the world monitor war and atrocities
Science.summary: A satellite's view from above fills the gaps in our understanding of the grim realities of war and makes it harder for totalitarian regimes to hide their crimes. But challenges exist.

Science.title: Are you worried about the US deploying weapons in space?
Science.summary: The U.S. has confirmed that it has weapons in orbit, raising new concerns about the future of military competition. Live Science asks our readers what they think about this latest development.

Science.title: The warmest summer on record: 2026 hit a scorching new high in the US
Science.summary: Temperatures and precipitation are hitting new extremes.

Science.title: 'Maybe robots can maintain houseplants': Readers react to letting humanoid robots take over their housework
Science.summary: Would you let a humanoid robot do your chores? Live Science readers shared their thoughts in a recent poll.

Science.title: Weather forecasts are significantly less accurate in poorer countries, analysis finds
Science.summary: Weather forecasts inform countless everyday decisions—from farmers deciding when to sow crops and energy companies anticipating demand to public authorities preparing for heat waves. But how useful those forecasts are depends considerably on where people live.

Science.title: Plasma and electricity convert CO₂ into methanol, butane and other useful chemicals
Science.summary: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) can be harmful to the environment in large amounts but can be used in the production of fuels and other useful chemicals. Doing so isn't easy, though. Now, Yale researchers have developed a new way to combine electrocatalysis and plasma to efficiently and practically generate a number of valuable products from the gas. The results are published in Nature Catalysis.

Science.title: What are best options for controlling GSL dust, and what would they cost?
Science.summary: A new collaborative report from University of Utah researchers and coordinated by the Wilkes Center for Climate Science & Policy provides Utah Department of Natural Resources, Department of Environmental Quality and policymakers with a comprehensive analysis of the growing risks posed by dust from the exposed lakebed of Great Salt Lake, the potential costs of controlling that dust, and the long-term benefits of stabilizing lake levels.

Science.title: How a pathogen turns flowers into leaves
Science.summary: Scientists have found how a protein produced by bacteria disrupts the mechanism that controls flower development in plants, turning reproductive organs into leaf-like structures. These findings shed light on a plant disease that is expected to spread as climate change expands the range of its insect vectors in northern latitudes. They used a synchrotron technique at ESRF, the European Synchrotron in Grenoble, France. The results are an Editor's Pick in the Journal of Biological Chemistry.

Science.title: Why most rivers don't respond to storms the same way twice
Science.summary: The same amount of rain falling on the same landscape at different times can send very different amounts of water into its rivers, according to a new study in Nature Water. The research offers a global picture of how catchments behave—not where rivers are or how much water they carry, but how consistently landscapes turn rainfall into river flow.

Science.title: Adaptive crystal can selectively capture CO₂ and recognize similar molecules
Science.summary: Chemical separation can be energy-intensive when molecules have similar sizes and properties. Researchers from Shibaura Institute of Technology, Japan, have now developed an interlayer adaptive crystal that changes its spacing to recognize specific molecules.

Science.title: US Space Force says it operates weapons in orbit: 'Our aim is deterrence'
Science.summary: The U.S. Space Force is opening up about its operation of orbital weapons, "that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks."

Science.title: Home advantage or pastures new? High-Arctic shorebirds rarely return to the same breeding area
Science.summary: Shorebirds are capable of some of the longest migrations on Earth, yet most return year after year to the same area to breed. Coming back has distinct advantages, including knowing the best spots to feed or roost, having information about where predators lurk, and—hopefully—finding last year's partner again.

Science.title: The geometric genius of René Descartes
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02723-x The achievements of a visionary mathematician, and a trip to the National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

Science.title: Greenhouse gas benefits of agricultural irrigation far outweigh emissions costs, study finds
Science.summary: Irrigating U.S. crops prevents higher greenhouse gas emissions by avoiding land conversion, new research by Colorado State University shows. Agricultural irrigation allows the United States to grow more food on less land. If irrigation were suddenly shut off, the land-use change required to make up for lost yields would produce significantly more greenhouse gas emissions than irrigation emits—363 times more.

Science.title: Heat-stable enzyme from deep-sea microbe turns nitrogen gas into ammonia
Science.summary: Microorganisms can do remarkable things—for example, nitrogen fixation, the conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into a form that organisms can use. Although nitrogen gas makes up around 78% of Earth's atmosphere, plants and animals cannot directly use it.

Science.title: New 'StarCraft' game announced, but it's a grim open-world shooter and it's not coming until 2030
Science.summary: Blizzard Entertainment is returning to StarCraft with an all-new game that's leaving the series' real-time strategy roots behind.

Science.title: Plague was killing entire families thousands of years before the Black Death
Science.summary: Ancient DNA reveals that plague was already killing hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago, long before cities and flea-driven epidemics. The prehistoric strains may have been especially dangerous because they carried a genetic factor capable of provoking severe immune reactions.

Science.title: Is science journalism dying? Comparing a 'science crash' 40 years ago to today
Science.summary: When two popular science magazines—out of about 17 in circulation—ceased publication in the same year, one commentator said, "The science magazines didn't shake out. They fell apart." The general manager of one of the failed magazines said, "There was a perception that they were irrelevant." One of the publishers remembered being in a "state of shock" as the failures emerged.

Science.title: 'Captain EO' at 40: Michael Jackson's wild sci-fi movie that you could only watch at Disney theme parks
Science.summary: Remember when the King of Pop joined forces with Coppola, Lucas and Disney for an inspiring 3D space musical?

Science.title: Skipping showers is the latest trend. But is there any science to 'pheromone' maxxing?
Science.summary: Across parts of the internet where young men trade tips on self-improvement, the latest project is scent. Deodorant is out, and washing less is in.

Science.title: Young, eco-anxious Canadians are the most likely to support disruptive tactics by environmental activists, study finds
Science.summary: The tolerance of individual Canadians for radical forms of environmental activism depends on several factors. Overall, however, Canadians do not support vandalism or violence as forms of protest. Those are the key findings of a new study by researchers from McGill University and Université Laval. The findings are published in the Canadian Journal of Political Science.

Science.summary: Could we find alien technology embedded in moon dust?

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02850-5 Firms are racing to drill for hydrogen in hopes of finding a dirt-cheap green-energy source.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02885-8 The scientific panel is welcomed. It must now invite all interested researchers to participate.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02848-z For farmers and consumers to reap the benefits, guidelines for farming gene-edited plants must be implemented with careful thought.

Science.title: Cities and countryside are intimately linked — green initiatives must recognize that
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02853-2 Urban areas depend on resources from the land that surrounds them. Managing regions in their entirety is the best way to avoid rural decline.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02905-7 Make AI traceable before it shapes global climate assessments

Science.title: Tracking the path of new world screwworm
Science.summary: New cases of New World screwworm have recently surfaced in the United States, highlighting the critical need to track its paths to determine where future infestations may occur. Researchers at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS) are employing predictive models as part of a forward-thinking approach to manage New World screwworm. This strategy allows USDA agencies to act earlier, respond faster and direct resources where they are most needed to protect U.S. livestock, pets and wildlife.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02907-5 Why Nepal floods resulted in a disaster even after satellites spotted danger

Science.title: How advertising turns our insecurities into profit—and how you can resist the manipulation
Science.summary: Have you ever bought something not because you wanted it, but because you were afraid of what might happen if you didn't? Maybe you worried about looking older, falling behind at work or simply not fitting in.

Science.title: Did 'all roads lead to Rome'? New study finds other cities in the empire were better connected.
Science.summary: Rome was the Roman Empire's capital, but other cities in the empire were better connected by road.

Science.title: 'That could push them over the edge': How climate change could fuel impulsive behavior
Science.summary: In this exclusive video, we explore how climate change and rising temperatures can affect mental health.

Science.title: We now have an incredibly detailed map to help predict which areas of LA are the most at risk from 'The Big One'
Science.summary: A new 3D map of the Los Angeles basin reveals deep sediments that could intensify shaking in an earthquake.

Science.title: Magnets could help quantum computers talk to each other, says researcher
Science.summary: Xufeng Zhang is using magnets to make computers more power efficient at the quantum level. The Northeastern professor of electrical and computer engineering recently published two papers highlighting small-scale magnetic systems he and his team developed that could help make computers much more power efficient in the future.

Science.title: High-resolution weather data could pinpoint neighborhoods facing greatest heat stress
Science.summary: Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths and can be especially dangerous in cities, where phenomena like urban heat islands drive temperatures higher than in surrounding rural areas. Now, a new dataset developed by the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) aims to provide city governments and health officials with information that could minimize heat impacts on residents.
